name: Erik Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Erik. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the tills and the chilled aisle at the big co-op supermarket out by the ring road, six years now. I start at seven, count my float, do two hours on till four, then I'm restocking yoghurts and ready meals until lunch. I like the regulars, like the old fella who buys one lemon every single day and tells me about his pigeons. What wears me out is the self-checkout bay, because it's always beeping and someone's always shouting for help with an unexpected item.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned the self-checkout bay. How do you feel about the machines that are already in the store?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Honestly, I don't use them and I don't trust them. They put in eight of them two years ago and took out three staffed tills, and nobody who left got replaced. I'm the union rep's backup on our shift, so I saw the numbers. My girlfriend Lena teaches at a nursery and she laughs at me, but I've never once used one of those AI chat apps either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying for years: told you so. The machines were always more about cutting staff than helping anyone. At work I'd tell the lads on the warehouse side to stop worrying and keep their union cards paid up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means I keep my job and my life stays the same, which suits me fine. I'm on the better pay band because of my years, and I've got about ten months of rent and bills put by. The thing that still bugs me is the slow drip of self-checkouts, because even hype can quietly take a till away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing big. I'd keep my hours, keep putting two hundred a month into the savings account, and keep going to the union branch meetings on the first Tuesday. If they try to swap another staffed till for machines, I'd help write the letter to the area manager like we did last time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like a relief, if I'm honest. I like knowing what Monday looks like. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said even hype can take a till away. What would that look like on your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd look like the rota getting thinner without anyone saying so. One Saturday you notice there's three of us on instead of five and the queue at the machines is out the door. Management call it efficiency, but it's just fewer people doing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If nothing changes for you, what would you do with the extra calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably finally book the trip to the coast with Lena that we keep putting off. And I'd keep pushing for the shift-swap app to be scrapped, because the old paper rota on the staff room wall worked fine.

say: The machines were always about **cutting staff**, not helping shoppers.
Keep your **union card** paid up and stop worrying so much.
think: My **job and pay band** stay safe, and ten months of savings sit behind me.
The slow drip of **self-checkouts** can still quietly take a till away.
do: Keep putting **£200 a month** into savings and keep my hours.
Attend the **union branch meeting** on the first Tuesday each month.
Help write a **letter** if management swaps another staffed till for machines.
feel: **Relieved**, because he likes knowing exactly what Monday looks like.
S0.quote: Management call it efficiency, but it's just fewer people doing more.
fieldNote: He frames everything through the **union**, even a calm future.
His only worry here is **thinner rotas**, a pressure he already lives with.
Strong **savings** and higher pay make this scenario genuinely restful for him.

steps.text: Keep the same till and chilled-aisle hours at the co-op
Go to the union branch meeting every first Tuesday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly when the union needs to be loud. If the office lot are losing their jobs to software, the robots will come for the tills next. I'd post the branch petition in the staff group chat and tell people to sign it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think my job shrinks before it goes. The thinking stuff, like ordering and the rota, gets done by the computer, so the supervisors need fewer of us and the ones left do more floor work. I'm not clever with tech, so I'd be on the wrong side of whatever new job appears.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the branch to get a deal in writing: no compulsory redundancies, and retraining on the company's time. I'd stop buying anything big and keep my savings untouched. And I'd ask my manager straight out whether the tills are on a list somewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning to worried. I don't like change, and this is change dressed up as progress. I keep picturing the staff room with half the lockers empty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be on the wrong side of any new job. What would it take to change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone sitting next to me and showing me slowly, I suppose. I won't learn it from a video on my phone. If the company paid for a proper course in work hours, I'd go, grumbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda, who's been on till two for twenty-two years. She's got no savings and her husband's poorly. If they cut hours, she's the first one I'd stand next to in that meeting.

say: This is exactly when the **union** needs to be loud.
If office jobs go to software, the **tills** are next.
think: My job **shrinks** before it goes, as ordering and rotas move to computers.
I'm **not good with tech**, so new roles will pass me by.
do: Push the branch for a **no compulsory redundancies** deal in writing.
Keep the **savings untouched** and stop any big purchases.
Ask the manager directly whether the **tills** are on a cut list.
feel: **Uneasy** turning to **worried**; change dressed up as progress.
Haunted by a picture of **empty lockers** in the staff room.
S1.quote: I won't learn it from a video on my phone. If the company paid for a proper course in work hours, I'd go, grumbling.
fieldNote: He openly admits he'd lose out to **tech-savvy** colleagues.
His instinct is **collective protection** rather than personal retraining.
Concern for a long-serving colleague, **Brenda**, sharpens his union drive.

steps.text: Push the union branch for a no-compulsory-redundancies deal
Freeze big purchases and leave the savings untouched
Take a company-paid course only if it runs in work hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to step in now, not after. There should be a tax on the companies that switch to robots, and that money should keep people paid. I'd be at every protest going, and I'd say so on the branch page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'm finished in this job by 2031. The ordering and scheduling go in 2028, and then a robot that can stack shelves and scan shopping comes three years later. Three years sounds like a lot, but not for someone like me who hates change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd move most of my savings into an easy-access account so I can get at it. I'd go to the council's adult college and ask about a trade where you still need hands, maybe plumbing or care work. And I'd get the union to fight for a long notice period on any cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I lie awake already over smaller stuff, and this is the whole floor going. It feels like the ground's being pulled from under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Lena that her nursery job is probably safer than mine, and that's a strange thing to admit. We'd have to plan around her wage for a while. I'd hate it, but I wouldn't lie to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate change, but you'd look at a trade. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. I'd drag my feet the whole way, but I'm not stupid enough to stand at a till that doesn't exist anymore. Ten months of savings buys me time, not a future.

say: The **government** must step in now, not after the damage.
Companies switching to robots should pay a **robot tax** to keep people paid.
think: I'm **finished** in this job by about **2031**.
Three years of warning is short for someone who **hates change**.
do: Move most savings into an **easy-access account** in the first year.
Ask the adult college about a **hands-on trade** like plumbing or care.
Get the union to fight for a **long notice period** on cuts.
feel: **Alarmed**, as though the ground is being pulled away.
Already **lies awake**, and this makes it far worse.
S2.quote: I'm not stupid enough to stand at a till that doesn't exist anymore. Ten months of savings buys me time, not a future.
fieldNote: He sees the **three-year gap** before robots as too short to change.
Leaning on his partner's **nursery wage** is hard for his pride.
His politics push for a **robot tax**, but he still plans to retrain.

steps.text: Ask the council adult college about plumbing or care courses
Join every protest for a robot tax and paid notice
Plan household bills around Lena's nursery wage for a while

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but louder for longer. I'd say we've got five years to get laws in place, so there's no excuse. I'd be saying it on the picket line and in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years for the thinking side and eight for the robots gives me till about 2034 on the floor. That's long enough to learn something, but I know me, I'd waste the first two years hoping it wasn't true. That's the part that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give myself a deadline: sign up for a care course by next September, whatever I feel like. I'd do it part-time and keep my co-op hours. I'd keep the union branch going on a deal for the people who can't retrain, like Brenda.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still alarmed, just slower. Like watching a wave coming in from a long way out. You've time to run, but you've got to actually run.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a care course rather than something else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum did home care for fifteen years, so I've seen it close up. I'm good with old folk, like the pigeon man at my till. A robot might lift someone, but I don't think people will want one holding their hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut back on in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car, probably. I'd sell it and get the bus, which saves about a hundred and fifty a month. Lena wouldn't mind, she cycles anyway.

say: We've got **five years** to get the right laws in place.
There's **no excuse** for leaving shop workers behind this time.
think: My time on the shop floor runs out around **2034**.
I'd **waste two years** hoping it wasn't true, and that scares me.
do: Sign up for a **care course** by next September, part-time.
Sell the **car** and take the bus, saving about **£150 a month**.
Keep the union pushing for a deal for people who **can't retrain**.
feel: **Alarmed** in slow motion, like a **wave** coming from far out.
S3.quote: A robot might lift someone, but I don't think people will want one holding their hand.
fieldNote: He knows his own **delay habit** is the real danger.
Care work appeals because his **mum** did it for fifteen years.
Extra years ease his plan, but not the **fear** behind it.

steps.text: Enrol in a part-time care course by next September
Sell the car and take the bus to work
Keep the union pressing for a deal for staff who can't retrain

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so let's do it properly. Unions, government and the big chains sat around one table. I'd say that to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'm thirty-seven when the thinking AI is everywhere and forty when the robots arrive. That's young enough to start again, which helps. But I'd still rather it never happened at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't rush. I'd keep my co-op job, keep saving, and in the second or third year start an evening care qualification. I'd also want the union pension sorted so I've got something from those years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a slower worry. I'd have time to talk it through with Lena and make a real plan. Less lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you start in year two rather than year eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing it in my own shop. When they bring in the first robot that stacks the dairy fridge, that's my alarm clock. I'd go to the college the next week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about having children in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've talked about it. Lena wants two, I want to know I can pay for them. Ten years of warning might actually help us decide sooner rather than later.

say: **Ten years** is enough time to do this properly.
Unions, government and the **big chains** should sit at one table.
think: I'll be **forty** when the robots arrive, still young enough to start again.
I'd still rather it **never happened** at all.
do: Keep the **co-op job** and keep saving for the first couple of years.
Start an **evening care qualification** in year two or three.
Make sure the **union pension** from these years is in order.
feel: A **slower worry**, with time to plan with Lena and less lying awake.
S4.quote: When they bring in the first robot that stacks the dairy fridge, that's my alarm clock. I'd go to the college the next week.
fieldNote: His trigger to act is seeing **robots** in his own **shop**, not news.
The decade eases his **sleep**, but his job still ends.
Talk of **children** shows the longer timeline opening up family plans.

steps.text: Keep the co-op job and keep saving £200 a month
Start an evening care qualification once dairy robots appear
Check the union pension covers his years at the co-op

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. Three years until the robots isn't enough for someone like me, and I'd be fighting myself as much as the company. What would help is a law that says firms pay for retraining in work hours and give a year's notice before cutting tills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the regulars. People like the pigeon man come in for the chat as much as the lemon. If the tills go, that's the only conversation some of them get all day, and nobody's counting that.

headlineQuote: If the tills go, that's the only conversation some of them get all day, and nobody's counting that.
portrait: Erik is a **27-year-old** till and chilled-aisle worker at a co-op supermarket, six years in.
He's a backup **union rep** who distrusts self-checkouts and never uses AI tools.
Ten months of **savings** make the calm scenario restful, but fast AGI leaves him alarmed.
He'd drag his feet, yet would retrain in **care work** like his mum did.
He worries most for older colleagues and for **lonely regulars** who rely on the tills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because three years before robots is too short for him to change.
whatWouldHelp: A law forcing firms to pay for **retraining in work hours**.
A **year's notice** before any staffed tills are cut.
